nameStory: The 'Green Arrow Arum' gets its name from its distinctive arrow-shaped leaves that point skyward like a hunter's arrow. Unlike many arums that have showy white or colorful flower parts, this species keeps things green and subtle, earning it the 'green' part of its name.
description: Green Arrow Arum is a wetland perennial that grows 1-3 feet tall with bold, arrow-shaped leaves emerging directly from the muddy ground. Its most distinctive feature is the dramatic pointed leaves that can be 8-16 inches long, resembling giant green arrowheads. In late spring, it produces a subtle greenish flower spike (called a spathe) that's easy to miss among the striking foliage. This is a true water-lover that thrives with its feet wet in marshes, swamps, and along pond edges.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, arrow-shaped leaves with prominent parallel veins running from base to tip - they feel thick and waxy to the touch, almost like leather when mature

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Leaves emerge directly from the ground on long stalks with no visible above-ground stem - the whole plant appears to rise straight up from the mud

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Greenish, cylindrical flower spike (spathe) that's partially enclosed by a green hood-like leaf - much less showy than the white spathes of Skunk Cabbage

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found with roots in standing water or very wet, mucky soil that squelches underfoot - never on dry land

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Green berries clustered on a thick spike that often bends down into the water when ripe - the berries feel firm and waxy

habitat: Green Arrow Arum thrives in New England's wettest spots - marshes, swamps, pond edges, and slow-moving stream banks where the soil stays saturated year-round. You'll find it growing alongside cattails, pickerelweed, and wild rice in areas that may flood seasonally. It prefers spots with rich, organic muck rather than sandy or rocky wetland edges.

seasonality.spring: New arrow-shaped leaves unfurl in late spring, growing rapidly once temperatures warm. The inconspicuous green flower spikes appear in May-June, hidden among the developing foliage.
seasonality.summer: Leaves reach full size and turn deep green with prominent veining clearly visible. Green berry clusters develop and ripen, often bending down toward the water surface by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back as temperatures drop, while ripe berries may persist into early fall before dropping into the water.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground rhizomes, leaving no above-ground trace until the following spring's emergence.

funFact: Green Arrow Arum has formed a fascinating partnership with tiny chloropid flies - the plant actually provides a nursery where the flies can lay their eggs and raise their young, and in return, the flies inadvertently pollinate the flowers as they go about their business!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young Pickerelweed, but Pickerelweed has heart-shaped leaf bases while Green Arrow Arum has distinctly pointed, triangular leaf bases. Memory trick: 'Arrow' points down at the base too - it's triangular all the way down, not heart-shaped.
contextualKnowledge: The alternate name 'Tuckahoe' comes from Native American usage - the starchy underground rhizomes were traditionally processed and used as food, though they require careful preparation as they contain calcium oxalate crystals that can cause mouth irritation if eaten raw.
compareHints: Green Arrow Arum is the only arrow arum species in New England, but it's most similar to other members of the arum family like Skunk Cabbage and Jack-in-the-Pulpit. Unlike those relatives with their showy white or striped flower parts, Green Arrow Arum keeps everything green and subtle. Its leaves are also much more distinctly arrow-shaped than the broad oval leaves of Skunk Cabbage or the compound leaves of Jack-in-the-Pulpit.
